class-11/biology/introduction-to-biology.centralConcept: Biology — the science of life, from molecule to biosphere

subtopics.name: Etymology and definition
points: From Greek bios (life) + logos (study): the study of living organisms and their interactions
A living thing is defined by a set of properties, not by one feature alone
Biology is a natural science built on observation, hypothesis, experiment and theory

subtopics.name: Defining properties of life
points: Growth, reproduction, metabolism, response to stimuli, homeostasis, cellular organisation
Viruses sit outside the definition: they reproduce only inside a host cell
Organisation is hierarchical: molecule -> organelle -> cell -> tissue -> organ -> organism -> population -> community -> ecosystem -> biosphere

branches.topic: Level 2 — Core: the branches of biology

subtopics.name: Structural and functional branches
points: Morphology (external form), anatomy (internal structure), histology (tissues), cytology (cells)
Physiology (functions), biochemistry (chemical basis), genetics (heredity), embryology (development)
Taxonomy (classification), ecology (organism-environment relations), evolution (descent with modification)

subtopics.name: Applied and interdisciplinary branches
points: Biotechnology, microbiology, immunology, pathology, pharmacology, agriculture, horticulture
Bioinformatics, biophysics, biomathematics, bioethics as modern interfaces
Nepal context: forestry, fisheries, apiculture and sericulture are applied branches of direct economic value

branches.topic: Level 3 — Upgraded: how biology is actually done

subtopics.name: Scientific method as a loop
points: Observation -> question -> hypothesis -> prediction -> controlled experiment -> analysis -> revision
A hypothesis must be falsifiable; a theory is a well-tested explanatory framework, not a guess
Controls and variables: independent (manipulated), dependent (measured), controlled (held constant)

subtopics.name: Modern scale of the field
points: About 8.7 million eukaryotic species estimated; roughly 1.5-2 million described so far
Genomics, CRISPR and single-cell sequencing moved biology from description to engineering
Model organisms (E. coli, yeast, Drosophila, Arabidopsis, zebrafish, mouse) carry most mechanistic work

subtopics.name: Common confusions
points: Botany/zoology are kingdom-scoped; microbiology cuts across kingdoms (bacteria, viruses, protozoa, fungi)
Anatomy is structure, physiology is function — do not swap them in a definition question
A theory is not weaker than a law: laws describe, theories explain

class-11/biology/introduction-to-biology.centralConcept: Biology as a hub science — borrowing methods from every other discipline

branches.topic: Level 1 — Foundation: why the connections exist

subtopics.name: Shared physical and chemical basis
points: All life obeys the same physics and chemistry: diffusion, osmosis, thermodynamics, bonding
Water's polarity and hydrogen bonding explain almost every transport and solvent property in cells
Carbon's tetravalency underwrites the whole diversity of organic molecules

subtopics.name: Biology with physical sciences
points: Biochemistry: reaction pathways, enzyme kinetics, energetics of ATP
Biophysics: membrane potentials, muscle mechanics, X-ray crystallography of DNA and proteins
Physical chemistry explains pH, buffers, colligative properties and osmosis in living systems

subtopics.name: Biology with formal sciences
points: Biomathematics: population growth models, epidemic curves, genetic ratios, statistical tests
Bioinformatics: sequence alignment, phylogenetics, database mining of genomes
Statistics is essential because biological variation is the norm, not the exception

subtopics.name: Biology with social and earth sciences
points: Geography and geology: biogeography, fossil record, soil formation, plate tectonics and species distribution
Psychology and neuroscience: behaviour, learning, reflex pathways
Economics and ethics: agriculture, conservation policy, bioethics of gene editing

branches.topic: Level 3 — Upgraded: convergence and its consequences

subtopics.name: From reduction to systems
points: Reductionism explains parts; systems biology explains how parts interact as networks
Omics layers stack: genome -> transcriptome -> proteome -> metabolome -> phenotype
Emergent properties (consciousness, ecosystem stability) cannot be read off a single molecule

subtopics.name: Ethical boundary
points: Recombinant DNA safety debate crystallised at the 1975 Asilomar conference
Bioethics now governs gene therapy, cloning, GMO release and human subject research
Scientific capability and social permission are separate questions

class-11/biology/introduction-to-biology.centralConcept: Scope of biology — breadth of scale and depth of specialisation

subtopics.name: Sub-cellular to organism
points: Molecular biology and biochemistry sit at the smallest scale
Cell biology, histology and anatomy build upward in organisation
Physiology and developmental biology explain function and formation of the whole organism

subtopics.name: Population to biosphere
points: Genetics and evolution explain variation and change across generations
Ecology spans organism, population, community, ecosystem and biosphere
Conservation biology applies ecological theory to preventing loss

branches.topic: Level 2 — Core: classical vs modern scope

subtopics.name: Classical fields
points: Taxonomy, morphology, anatomy, embryology, palaeontology — largely descriptive origins
Systematics organises diversity into a predictive phylogenetic framework
Economic botany and zoology catalogued useful species

subtopics.name: Modern fields
points: Molecular biology, genomics, proteomics, metabolomics
Immunology, neurobiology, stem cell biology, synthetic biology
Bioinformatics and computational biology as the analysis layer over all of the above

branches.topic: Level 3 — Upgraded: where the frontier is

subtopics.name: Engineering life
points: CRISPR-Cas9 made targeted genome editing routine and cheap
Synthetic biology designs circuits and organisms rather than only studying them
mRNA platform technology compressed vaccine development from years to months

subtopics.name: Scope limits
points: Biology cannot yet predict phenotype from genotype in most complex traits
Ecosystem-level prediction remains weak because interactions are nonlinear
Ethical and regulatory scope always trails technical scope

class-11/biology/introduction-to-biology.centralConcept: Interdependence of biology with other sciences

subtopics.name: No science is isolated
points: Living systems are physical-chemical systems, so biology inherits their laws
Measurement, modelling and statistics come from mathematics
Earth processes set the stage on which evolution and ecology operate

subtopics.name: Chemistry interface
points: Organic chemistry explains biomolecule structure and reactivity
Enzyme catalysis, pH and buffers are applied physical chemistry
Analytical chemistry (chromatography, spectroscopy) supplies the measurement tools

subtopics.name: Physics interface
points: Optics underlies microscopy; electron microscopy resolved organelles
Mechanics and fluid dynamics explain circulation, locomotion and plant water transport
Radioisotopes and radiation are both tools (tracers, imaging) and hazards (mutation)

subtopics.name: Mathematics and computing interface
points: Mendelian ratios are probability; population genetics is algebra and calculus
Sequence alignment and phylogenetics are algorithmic problems
Epidemiological models (SIR-type) guide public health decisions

subtopics.name: Convergence examples
points: X-ray crystallography (physics) plus chemistry solved the DNA double helix in 1953
PCR (chemistry) plus computation built modern diagnostics and forensics
Optogenetics combines optics, genetics and neurophysiology

subtopics.name: Why it matters for exams
points: Interdisciplinary questions are increasingly common in entrance papers
Answer with the mechanism from the borrowing science, then the biological consequence
Naming the interface explicitly earns marks that a vague answer does not

branches.topic: Level 1 — Foundation: the four macromolecule classes

subtopics.name: Carbohydrates
points: Monosaccharides (glucose, fructose), disaccharides (sucrose, lactose), polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose)
Primary quick energy source; cellulose is structural and indigestible to humans
General formula (CH2O)n; glycosidic bonds link monomers

subtopics.name: Proteins
points: Built from 20 amino acids joined by peptide bonds
Four structure levels: primary sequence, secondary (alpha helix, beta sheet), tertiary (3D fold), quaternary (subunits)
Functions: enzymes, transport, structure, signalling, immunity, movement

subtopics.name: Lipids
points: Fats, oils, phospholipids, steroids, waxes; hydrophobic or amphipathic
Highest energy density per gram; phospholipids form the bilayer
Cholesterol modulates membrane fluidity and is a steroid hormone precursor

subtopics.name: Nucleic acids
points: DNA stores information; RNA transmits and executes it
Nucleotides = pentose sugar + phosphate + nitrogenous base
DNA is double-stranded with A-T and G-C pairing; RNA is usually single-stranded with uracil

subtopics.name: How shape creates function
points: Enzyme active site geometry gives substrate specificity (lock-and-key, induced fit)
Protein denaturation destroys function by destroying tertiary shape, not primary sequence
Saturated vs unsaturated fatty acid tails change membrane packing and fluidity

subtopics.name: Minerals and water
points: Water: universal solvent, high specific heat, high latent heat, cohesion and adhesion
Macro-minerals (Ca, P, K, Na, Mg, S, Cl) and micro-minerals (Fe, Zn, Cu, I, Mn) in trace amounts
Iron in haemoglobin, iodine in thyroxine, calcium in bone and clotting

branches.topic: Level 3 — Upgraded: quantitative and modern view

subtopics.name: Energetics
points: Carbohydrate ~4 kcal/g, protein ~4 kcal/g, lipid ~9 kcal/g
ATP is the universal energy currency; ~30.5 kJ/mol released on hydrolysis under standard conditions
Energy is transferred, never created — the whole chain traces back to photosynthesis

subtopics.name: Tests and identification
points: Benedict's test: reducing sugars give brick-red precipitate on heating
Biuret test: proteins give violet; Sudan III stains lipids red
Iodine test: starch turns blue-black

subtopics.name: Frequently missed
points: Cellulose and starch are both glucose polymers but differ in glycosidic linkage and digestibility
Lipids are not polymers in the strict sense — they are not built from repeating identical units
DNA and RNA differ in sugar (deoxyribose vs ribose) and one base (thymine vs uracil)

class-11/biology/biomolecules-and-cell-b.centralConcept: Biomolecules and enzymes — the chemistry of the living cell

subtopics.name: Micromolecules vs macromolecules
points: Micromolecules: small, low molecular weight, soluble — sugars, amino acids, nucleotides, minerals, water
Macromolecules: large, high molecular weight — polysaccharides, proteins, nucleic acids
Acid-insoluble pool (macromolecules) vs acid-soluble pool (micromolecules) is the classical operational split

subtopics.name: Elemental composition
points: C, H, O, N are the dominant elements of life; S and P are next
Carbon is tetravalent and forms stable chains and rings — the backbone of organic chemistry
Water is the most abundant molecule in any cell (60-90% of fresh mass)

subtopics.name: Enzyme fundamentals
points: Almost all enzymes are proteins; ribozymes are catalytic RNA exceptions
They lower activation energy without changing the equilibrium position
Specificity comes from active site complementarity to the substrate

subtopics.name: Factors affecting enzyme activity
points: Temperature: rate rises to an optimum then falls sharply as denaturation begins
pH: each enzyme has an optimum; extremes denature
Substrate concentration saturates at Vmax; inhibitors (competitive, non-competitive) change Km or Vmax differently

subtopics.name: Coenzymes and cofactors
points: Cofactors are non-protein helpers: metal ions (Mg2+, Zn2+, Fe2+) or organic coenzymes
NAD, FAD and coenzyme A are organic coenzymes derived from vitamins
Apoenzyme + cofactor = holoenzyme (the active form)

subtopics.name: Beyond the lock-and-key
points: Induced fit: the active site reshapes on binding, explaining broad substrate tolerance
Allosteric regulation lets a distant site control activity — the basis of metabolic feedback
Enzyme cascades amplify signals (blood clotting, complement, hormone action)

subtopics.name: Water as a biomolecule
points: High specific heat stabilises body temperature; high latent heat of vaporisation powers cooling
Cohesion and adhesion drive transpiration pull in xylem
Water is the medium for every biochemical reaction and a reactant in hydrolysis

subtopics.name: The four classes at a glance
points: Carbohydrates: immediate energy and structure
Proteins: catalysis, transport, structure, defence
Lipids: energy storage, membranes, hormones
Nucleic acids: information storage and transfer

subtopics.name: Why each class exists
points: Carbohydrates are easily oxidised, giving rapid ATP without oxygen debt
Proteins are the only class that catalyses reactions, so they carry regulation
Lipids store the most energy per gram and form the only barrier that makes a cell a cell
Nucleic acids are the only class that can be copied with high fidelity

subtopics.name: Minerals and water
points: Macro-minerals are needed in gram quantities; micro-minerals in milligram or microgram quantities
Deficiency diseases map to specific minerals: iodine -> goitre, iron -> anaemia, calcium -> rickets
Water makes up the majority of protoplasm and is the solvent for all metabolism

subtopics.name: Metabolic interconnection
points: Excess carbohydrate converts to glycogen, then to fat — the classes interconvert
Amino acids can enter respiration as keto acids after deamination
Nucleotides are built from amino acid, sugar and phosphate precursors

class-11/biology/biomolecules-and-cell-b.centralConcept: The cell — structural and functional unit of life

subtopics.name: Historical development
points: Robert Hooke (1665) coined 'cell' after observing cork under a compound microscope
Anton van Leeuwenhoek first saw living cells (bacteria, protozoa)
Schleiden and Schwann (1838-39) proposed that plants and animals are made of cells; Virchow (1855) added omnis cellula e cellula

subtopics.name: Modern cell theory
points: All living organisms are composed of one or more cells
The cell is the basic unit of structure and function
All cells arise from pre-existing cells by division
Cells contain hereditary material passed to daughter cells

subtopics.name: Prokaryotic cell
points: No membrane-bound nucleus; DNA is a single circular chromosome in the nucleoid
No membrane-bound organelles; ribosomes are 70S
Cell wall usually present (peptidoglycan in bacteria); may have capsule, flagella, pili, plasmids

subtopics.name: Eukaryotic cell
points: True nucleus bounded by a double membrane with pores
Membrane-bound organelles: mitochondria, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, plastids
Ribosomes are 80S; extensive internal membrane system allows compartmentalised chemistry

branches.topic: Level 3 — Upgraded: size, shape and scale

subtopics.name: Dimensions
points: Typical prokaryote 1-10 micrometre; typical eukaryote 10-100 micrometre
Surface area to volume ratio limits cell size — larger cells must divide or become flattened
Human red blood cell ~7 micrometre; a frog egg ~1 mm is near the practical single-cell ceiling

subtopics.name: Cell as an open system
points: Cells exchange matter and energy continuously with the environment
Compartmentalisation lets incompatible reactions run simultaneously
The endosymbiotic theory explains mitochondria and chloroplasts as captured prokaryotes

subtopics.name: Frequently missed
points: Prokaryotes DO have ribosomes — they lack membrane-bound organelles, not all organelles
Viruses are not cells: no cytoplasm, no metabolism, no independent reproduction
Cell theory's classical form predates the discovery of viruses and does not cover them

subtopics.name: The single decisive difference
points: A membrane-bound nucleus is the defining eukaryotic feature
Everything else (organelles, size, chromosome number) follows from that compartmentalisation
Prokaryotes = Bacteria and Archaea; eukaryotes = Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia

subtopics.name: Genetic apparatus
points: Prokaryote: single circular DNA, no histones (archaea have histone-like proteins), no nucleolus
Eukaryote: multiple linear chromosomes with histones, organised into chromatin, distinct nucleolus
Prokaryotes often carry plasmids — small extrachromosomal circular DNA

subtopics.name: Membranes and organelles
points: Prokaryote: plasma membrane only, no ER/Golgi/lysosome/mitochondrion
Eukaryote: extensive endomembrane system plus double-membrane organelles
Both have ribosomes, but 70S vs 80S — the basis of antibiotic selectivity

subtopics.name: Division and reproduction
points: Prokaryote: binary fission, no mitosis or meiosis, no spindle
Eukaryote: mitosis for growth, meiosis for gametes
Prokaryotes exchange genes by transformation, transduction and conjugation

subtopics.name: Why it matters medically
points: 70S vs 80S ribosome difference lets antibiotics (streptomycin, tetracycline) hit bacteria without harming human cells
Peptidoglycan cell wall is the target of penicillin — absent in human cells
Rapid binary fission plus horizontal gene transfer drives antibiotic resistance

subtopics.name: Evolutionary reading
points: Prokaryotes appeared ~3.5 billion years ago; eukaryotes ~1.5-2 billion years ago
Endosymbiosis converted engulfed bacteria into mitochondria and chloroplasts
Prokaryotes still dominate biomass and biochemical diversity

class-11/biology/biomolecules-and-cell-b.centralConcept: Organelles — division of labour inside the eukaryotic cell

subtopics.name: Single-membrane organelles
points: Endoplasmic reticulum (rough and smooth), Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, vacuoles, peroxisomes
These form the endomembrane system and handle synthesis, modification, transport and digestion
Vesicles shuttle cargo between them

subtopics.name: Double-membrane organelles
points: Mitochondria — aerobic respiration, cristae increase surface area
Plastids in plants — chloroplasts for photosynthesis, leucoplasts for storage, chromoplasts for pigment
Nuclear envelope with pores is also double

subtopics.name: Non-membrane organelles
points: Ribosomes (protein synthesis), centrioles (spindle formation in animal cells)
Cytoskeleton: microtubules, microfilaments, intermediate filaments
Cilia and flagella built on the 9+2 microtubule arrangement

subtopics.name: Protein pathway
points: Rough ER -> transport vesicle -> Golgi (modification, sorting, packaging) -> vesicle -> destination
Signal peptide directs a ribosome to the rough ER
Lysosomes are the terminal digestive compartment, formed from Golgi vesicles

subtopics.name: Energy organelles
points: Mitochondrion: outer membrane, inner membrane folded into cristae, matrix with Krebs enzymes and own DNA
Chloroplast: thylakoid stacks (grana) for light reactions, stroma for Calvin cycle
Both are semi-autonomous: own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes

subtopics.name: Surface area engineering
points: Cristae fold the inner mitochondrial membrane to pack in electron transport chain complexes
Thylakoid stacking packs photosystems into a small volume
Microvilli and ER folding follow the same principle: maximise membrane area in fixed volume

subtopics.name: Cell-type specialisation
points: Pancreatic cells are rich in rough ER; muscle cells are rich in mitochondria
Mature mammalian red blood cells lose nucleus and organelles to maximise haemoglobin capacity
Organelle abundance is a diagnostic clue to cell function

subtopics.name: Plasma membrane
points: Fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972): phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins
Selectively permeable; controls what enters and leaves
Cholesterol and unsaturated tails tune fluidity

subtopics.name: Cell wall (plants, fungi)
points: Plant cell wall is mainly cellulose; fungal walls are chitin
Provides rigidity, prevents bursting under osmotic pressure
Middle lamella, primary wall and secondary wall layers

subtopics.name: Nucleus
points: Nuclear envelope with pores controls nucleocytoplasmic traffic
Nucleolus is the ribosome assembly site
Chromatin is DNA plus histone proteins

subtopics.name: Cytoplasm and cytoskeleton
points: Cytosol is the aqueous matrix for glycolysis and many reactions
Microtubules give tracks for vesicle transport; microfilaments drive shape change and cytokinesis
Cytoskeleton maintains polarity and organelle positioning

subtopics.name: Diagnostic differences
points: Plant cells: cellulose wall, large central vacuole, chloroplasts, no centrioles in most higher plants
Animal cells: no wall, no chloroplasts, centrioles present, small temporary vacuoles
Both share nucleus, mitochondria, ER, Golgi, ribosomes, cytoskeleton

subtopics.name: Transport across membranes
points: Passive: simple diffusion and facilitated diffusion (no ATP)
Active: pumps such as Na+/K+-ATPase move ions against gradients using ATP
Bulk transport: endocytosis and exocytosis via vesicles

subtopics.name: Cell membrane detail
points: Phospholipid bilayer ~7-8 nm thick; hydrophilic heads outward, hydrophobic tails inward
Integral proteins span the bilayer; peripheral proteins sit on one face
Glycoproteins and glycolipids on the outer surface form the glycocalyx used in recognition

subtopics.name: Cell wall detail
points: Cellulose microfibrils in a hemicellulose and pectin matrix
Primary wall is thin and extensible; secondary wall is thick and lignified
Plasmodesmata are channels through walls connecting adjacent plant cells

subtopics.name: Mitochondria and plastids
points: Mitochondrion: outer membrane, inner membrane with cristae, intermembrane space, matrix
Chloroplast: outer and inner membrane, stroma, thylakoid membranes stacked into grana
Both contain circular DNA and 70S ribosomes — evidence of endosymbiotic origin

subtopics.name: Endomembrane organelles
points: Rough ER studded with ribosomes for protein synthesis; smooth ER for lipid synthesis and detoxification
Golgi: cis and trans faces, glycosylation and sorting
Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes at acidic pH; peroxisomes handle hydrogen peroxide

subtopics.name: Nucleus and chromosomes
points: Nuclear envelope is double with pores; nucleolus makes rRNA
Chromatin is nucleosomes (DNA wound on histone octamers)
Chromosome number is species-specific and constant

subtopics.name: Cilia and flagella
points: 9+2 microtubule arrangement: nine doublets around a central pair
Dynein motors generate sliding that produces bending
Cilia are short and numerous; flagella are long and few

subtopics.name: Compartment logic
points: Each organelle maintains a distinct internal pH and enzyme set
Lysosomal enzymes work at ~pH 5, protecting the cytosol at pH ~7.2
Membrane identity is set by lipid composition and surface protein markers

subtopics.name: Cell inclusions
points: Non-living accumulations: starch grains, oil droplets, pigment granules, crystals
Glycogen granules in liver and muscle
Inclusions are storage or waste, not organelles

class-11/biology/biomolecules-and-cell-b.centralConcept: Eukaryotic organelles — structure and function in detail

subtopics.name: Boundary and framework
points: Cell wall gives shape and osmotic protection; membrane controls exchange
Cytoskeleton provides internal architecture and movement
Compartmentalisation is the organising principle of the eukaryotic cell

subtopics.name: Energy transduction
points: Mitochondria convert chemical energy of glucose into ATP via Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation
Chloroplasts convert light energy into chemical energy in photosynthesis
Both use chemiosmosis across a membrane to make ATP

subtopics.name: Synthesis and secretion
points: Ribosomes translate mRNA into polypeptide
ER folds and modifies; Golgi sorts and packages
Secretory vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane in exocytosis

subtopics.name: Digestion and recycling
points: Lysosomes digest worn organelles (autophagy) and ingested material (heterophagy)
Peroxisomes neutralise hydrogen peroxide and oxidise fatty acids
Autophagy recycles components under starvation

subtopics.name: Disease links
points: Mitochondrial DNA mutations cause maternally inherited disorders (e.g. MELAS)
Lysosomal storage diseases follow from a single defective hydrolytic enzyme
Defects in cilia (ciliopathies) impair mucus clearance and development

subtopics.name: Phases
points: Interphase (G1, S, G2) occupies most of the cycle; M phase is short
S phase is where DNA replicates
G0 is a non-dividing resting state some cells enter permanently

subtopics.name: Types of division
points: Amitosis: direct division without spindle, seen in prokaryotes and some lower eukaryotes
Mitosis: equational division producing two genetically identical diploid cells
Meiosis: reductional division producing four haploid gametes

subtopics.name: Prophase to telophase
points: Prophase: chromosomes condense, spindle forms, nuclear envelope breaks down
Metaphase: chromosomes align at the equator; anaphase: sister chromatids separate to poles
Telophase: nuclear envelopes reform; cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm

subtopics.name: Significance
points: Maintains chromosome number across generations of somatic cells
Underlies growth, repair and asexual reproduction
Genetic constancy is preserved because DNA is replicated before division

subtopics.name: Regulation
points: Cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases drive cell cycle progression
Checkpoints at G1/S, G2/M and metaphase verify DNA integrity and spindle attachment
Loss of checkpoint control leads to uncontrolled proliferation

subtopics.name: Consequences of error
points: Non-disjunction produces aneuploid gametes (e.g. trisomy 21)
Uncontrolled mitosis is the cellular basis of cancer
Apoptosis is programmed death that removes damaged cells

class-11/biology/biomolecules-and-cell-b.centralConcept: Cell cycle, mitosis and meiosis — and why both exist

subtopics.name: The cycle
points: Interphase: G1 (growth), S (DNA replication), G2 (preparation)
M phase: nuclear division (karyokinesis) then cytoplasmic division (cytokinesis)
Duration varies by cell type; human epithelial cells cycle in roughly 24 hours

subtopics.name: Mitosis
points: One division, two diploid daughter cells identical to the parent
Homologous chromosomes do not pair; no crossing over
Purpose: growth, repair, asexual reproduction

subtopics.name: Meiosis
points: Two successive divisions, four haploid daughter cells
Meiosis I is reductional: homologous chromosomes pair, cross over and separate
Meiosis II is equational: sister chromatids separate
Purpose: gamete formation and generation of genetic variation

subtopics.name: Sources of variation in meiosis
points: Crossing over in prophase I recombines maternal and paternal segments
Independent assortment of homologues at metaphase I gives 2^n combinations
Random fertilisation adds a further layer of variation

subtopics.name: Why both are necessary
points: Mitosis preserves; meiosis varies — a species needs both stability and diversity
Without meiosis, chromosome number would double every generation in sexual reproduction
Variation from meiosis is the raw material natural selection acts on

subtopics.name: Quantitative anchors
points: Human diploid number 2n = 46; haploid n = 23
Independent assortment in humans gives 2^23 = 8,388,608 combinations before crossing over
Meiosis produces four cells; mitosis produces two

subtopics.name: Frequently missed
points: DNA replicates once but the cell divides twice in meiosis
Crossing over happens in prophase I, not prophase II
Sister chromatids separate in anaphase of mitosis AND anaphase II of meiosis — homologues separate in anaphase I

class-11/biology/biomolecules-and-cell-b.centralConcept: Cell cycle and the three modes of division

subtopics.name: Direct division
points: Nucleus constricts and splits without spindle formation or chromosome condensation
Seen in prokaryotes and some lower eukaryotes and in pathological conditions
Produces genetically imprecise results compared with mitosis

branches.topic: Level 2 — Core: mitosis and meiosis stages

subtopics.name: Mitosis in order
points: Prophase: condensation, spindle formation, nuclear envelope breakdown
Metaphase: alignment at the metaphase plate
Anaphase: chromatid separation; Telophase: nuclear reformation and cytokinesis

subtopics.name: Meiosis I and II
points: Prophase I has five substages: leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, diakinesis
Pachytene is where crossing over occurs, forming chiasmata
Meiosis II mirrors mitosis but starts from haploid cells

subtopics.name: Biological roles
points: Mitosis maintains genetic constancy and enables repair
Meiosis halves chromosome number and generates variation
Amitosis is a simple but error-prone alternative

subtopics.name: Applied relevance
points: Cancer is a failure of mitotic control
Down syndrome arises from meiotic non-disjunction of chromosome 21
Tissue culture and cloning depend on controlled mitosis

class-11/biology/biomolecules-and-cell-b.centralConcept: Ecology and ecosystems — organisms in context

subtopics.name: Definitions
points: Ecology studies interactions between organisms and their environment
An ecosystem is a functional unit of biotic and abiotic components interacting
Levels: organism -> population -> community -> ecosystem -> biosphere

subtopics.name: Structure and function
points: Structural: producers, consumers, decomposers, trophic levels
Functional: energy flow (unidirectional) and nutrient cycling (biogeochemical)
Food chains and webs map the transfer pathways

subtopics.name: Ecosystem types
points: Aquatic: pond, lake, river, ocean
Terrestrial: forest, grassland, desert, tundra
Nepal spans Terai, hill and alpine ecosystems with distinct communities

subtopics.name: Energy and matter
points: Energy flows one way and is lost as heat at each transfer (~10% rule)
Matter cycles repeatedly through biogeochemical pathways
Productivity (GPP, NPP) measures the rate of energy capture

class-11/biology/biomolecules-and-cell-b.centralConcept: Environmental science — managing the human-nature interface

subtopics.name: Scope
points: Interdisciplinary study of the environment and human impact on it
Draws on ecology, chemistry, geology, economics and policy
Sustainability means meeting present needs without compromising future capacity

subtopics.name: Major issues
points: Pollution of air, water and soil
Climate change from greenhouse gas accumulation
Biodiversity loss and habitat fragmentation
Resource depletion: water, soil, fossil fuels

subtopics.name: Responses
points: Reduce, reuse, recycle; waste segregation and treatment
Renewable energy transition and energy efficiency
Protected areas, environmental legislation and EIA

subtopics.name: Nepal-specific
points: Glacier retreat threatens Himalayan water security
Community forestry is a globally cited success in forest recovery
Rapid urbanisation strains waste and water systems in the Kathmandu valley

subtopics.name: Darwin's logic
points: Individuals vary; more offspring are produced than can survive
Variants with advantageous traits survive and reproduce more
Over generations the population's trait distribution shifts

subtopics.name: Mechanisms
points: Natural selection, sexual selection, mutation, gene flow, genetic drift
Selection acts on phenotypes, changing allele frequencies
Speciation follows reproductive isolation

subtopics.name: Evidence
points: Fossil record, comparative anatomy (homologous and analogous structures)
Embryology, biogeography, molecular homology
Observed contemporary evolution: antibiotic resistance, industrial melanism

subtopics.name: Modern synthesis
points: Neo-Darwinism fuses selection with Mendelian genetics and population genetics
Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium describes conditions under which allele frequencies do not change
Fitness is relative reproductive success, not strength

subtopics.name: Terminology
points: Gene, allele, genotype, phenotype, homozygous, heterozygous
Dominant allele masks recessive in the heterozygote
Mendel's pea experiments established quantitative inheritance

subtopics.name: Law of segregation
points: Two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation
Each gamete carries only one allele
Explains the 3:1 monohybrid phenotypic ratio

subtopics.name: Law of independent assortment
points: Alleles of different genes assort independently when on different chromosomes
Explains the 9:3:3:1 dihybrid ratio
Fails for linked genes on the same chromosome

subtopics.name: Deviation: incomplete dominance and codominance
points: Incomplete dominance gives an intermediate phenotype (1:2:1)
Codominance expresses both alleles fully (AB blood group)
Multiple alleles and polygenic traits add further complexity

subtopics.name: Beyond Mendel
points: Linkage and crossing over break independent assortment
Sex-linked inheritance explains X-linked disorders such as haemophilia
Epistasis and polygenic inheritance explain continuous traits

subtopics.name: Quantitative anchors
points: Monohybrid F2 phenotypic ratio 3:1, genotypic 1:2:1
Dihybrid F2 phenotypic ratio 9:3:3:1
Test cross with a homozygous recessive reveals an unknown genotype

class-11/biology/biomolecules-and-cell-b.centralConcept: Homeostasis — keeping the internal environment stable

subtopics.name: Definition
points: Homeostasis maintains internal conditions within narrow limits despite external change
Controlled variables include temperature, pH, blood glucose, water and ion balance
Failure of homeostasis is the basis of most disease

subtopics.name: Negative feedback
points: A deviation triggers a response that reverses it
Receptor -> control centre -> effector loop
Examples: thermoregulation, blood glucose via insulin and glucagon, osmoregulation via ADH

subtopics.name: Positive feedback
points: Amplifies a deviation rather than reversing it
Examples: oxytocin in childbirth, blood clotting cascade
Usually self-limiting and tied to a definite endpoint

subtopics.name: System integration
points: Nervous control is fast and short-lived; endocrine control is slower and sustained
Liver, kidney, lungs and skin are the main homeostatic organs
Set points can be reset (fever raises the hypothalamic set point)

class-11/biology/biomolecules-and-cell-b.centralConcept: Biotechnology applications and their ethical limits

subtopics.name: What biotechnology is
points: Using living organisms or their components to make useful products
Traditional (fermentation, selective breeding) vs modern (recombinant DNA, gene editing)
Core tools: restriction enzymes, vectors, host cells, transformation

subtopics.name: Medicine
points: Recombinant insulin, growth hormone, interferons, vaccines
Gene therapy for monogenic disorders
Monoclonal antibodies for diagnosis and treatment

subtopics.name: Agriculture
points: Bt crops with built-in pest resistance
Golden rice as biofortification
Tissue culture and micropropagation for rapid clonal multiplication

subtopics.name: Ethical concerns
points: GMO release: gene flow to wild relatives and effects on non-target species
Germline gene editing is heritable and widely considered off-limits
Equity of access: patented medicines and smallholder dependence on seed companies
Biosafety regulation and informed consent are the governance responses
